For tangent, it's a bit different. The identity for tangent is: 
\[ \tan(-\theta) = -\tan(\theta) \]

So, unlike cosine which remains the same, the tangent function changes sign when you change the sign of the angle. Think of it like a mirror reflection - if you reflect a point across the y-axis, the x-coordinate (which is related to the tangent) will change sign.
so thisi is different so sin?

The identity for sine is similar to tangent:
\[ \sin(-\theta) = -\sin(\theta) \]

So, like tangent, the sine function also changes sign when you change the sign of the angle. This makes sense, because sine is an odd function, just like tangent. 

To remember it, you can think of the phrase "sine and tangent are odd, cosine is even" - it might help you recall these identities!

That's correct. The identity for tangent can also be written as:
\[ \tan(\theta) = -\tan(-\theta) \]

This is equivalent to the one I mentioned earlier: 
\[ \tan(-\theta) = -\tan(\theta) \]

Well done for spotting the alternative way to write it!

Sine is an odd function. This means that:
\[ \sin(-\theta) = -\sin(\theta) \]

So, sine is odd, not even. Remember, "sine and tangent are odd, cosine is even"!
